title: Harvard, If You're Listening
author: Terry Yu
summary: This article examines Harvard's 2026 decision to cap undergraduate A-grades at 60% of courses, situating it within the long-running story of grade inflation at elite American universities. Terry Yu marshals data including the 2024 Nation's Report Card showing twelfth-grade reading scores at record lows even as college enrollment rates rose, arguing that K-12 grade inflation has inflated the very pipeline Harvard cites when defending its high grades. The piece makes a distinction between Harvard's exceptionally strong incoming cohort and the broader national pattern of declining academic preparation, noting that the two are often conflated in public debates. Yu ultimately argues that Harvard's reform should be welcomed but is incomplete: the cap addresses the symptom without confronting either the institutional incentives that produced grade inflation or its downstream effects on curricular rigor. The article situates Harvard's action within a multi-decade pattern of institutional avoidance and asks whether a grade cap alone can restore the signal value grades are supposed to carry.
points: Harvard's own 2025 internal report found 60% of grades were A's by 2024-25, up from 25% two decades earlier — a dramatic self-indictment that finally forced institutional action in the form of a Fall 2027 grade cap.

K-12 grade inflation has complicated the familiar defense of elite university grade inflation: if the incoming pipeline itself reflects inflated credentials, the claim that students 'deserve' high grades because of their records becomes circular.

National twelfth-grade reading scores hit record lows in 2024 even as college acceptance rates rose — a paradox that suggests the college-going rate and actual academic preparation have increasingly decoupled.

A grade cap addresses the symptom but not the incentive structure that produced inflation: faculty discomfort with low grades, student evaluations tied to leniency, and reputational competition among peer institutions all remain untouched.

When the A becomes the expected baseline rather than the exceptional achievement, the transcript loses its information value for employers, graduate schools, and the students themselves — the core problem a cap alone cannot solve.
quotes: Grade inflation is among the oldest running complaints in American higher education, and for nearly as long, it has been understood as a problem concentrated at elite private universities.

At Harvard, Undergraduate Dean Claybaugh's (2025) internal report found that 60 percent of grades were A's by 2024-25, up from 25 percent two decades, the finding that prompted the cap on the issuance of A grades in undergraduate courses to be implemented in Fall, 2027.

The 2024 Nation's Report Card found that twelfth-grade average reading scores fell to their lowest level on record—3 points below 2019 and 10 points below the first such assessment in 1992—even as more seniors than before reported being accepted to a four-year college while fewer were apparently academically prepared for it.

Faculty attitudes about teaching and grading underwent a profound shift that coincided with the Vietnam War. Many professors, certainly not all or even a majority, became convinced that grades were not a useful tool for motivation, were not a valid means of evaluation and created a harmful authoritarian environment for learning.

At Yale, a faculty report found that 78.97 percent of undergraduate grades in 2022-2023 fell in the A-range, with the mean GPA rising to 3.70. At Brown, 67 percent of grades were A's in 2020-21, up from 39 percent in 1993.

The decline, however, was not evenly distributed: scores fell across most of the distribution but held steady among the highest-performing students at the 90th percentile, even as a record 32 percent of seniors scored below NAEP Basic in reading.
